questions.q: In the kinetic particle model of matter, temperature is a measure of which property of a substance's particles?
options: The total internal energy of all the particles added together
The average translational kinetic energy of the particles
The potential energy stored in the attractive forces between particles
The combined rotational and vibrational kinetic energy of the molecules
questions.explanation: Temperature is a measure of the average translational kinetic energy of the particles. The other contributions to the internal energy — potential, rotational and vibrational energy — do not affect the temperature, which is why a melting or boiling substance can absorb energy without its temperature changing.

questions.q: How is the specific heat capacity of a substance defined?
options: The total energy stored in 1 kg of the substance
The amount of energy required to increase the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 °C (or 1 K)
The energy required to change the state of 1 kg of the substance from solid to liquid
The energy required to raise any mass of the substance by 1 °C
questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity is defined as the amount of energy required to increase the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 °C (or 1 K, since the degree sizes match). A high specific heat capacity means the material increases in temperature slowly when heated, and cools slowly.

questions.q: Using Table 11.3, water has a specific heat capacity of about 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Why does this make water heat up and cool down more slowly than most common materials?
options: Water particles move faster than those of other substances at the same temperature
It takes more energy to increase the temperature of water by 1 °C than for almost any other common substance, so water maintains its temperature well
Water has a lower mass per particle, so it stores less energy
Water's specific heat capacity is lower than that of metals such as copper
questions.explanation: It takes more energy to increase the temperature of water by 1 °C than any other common substance, and water also needs to lose more energy to decrease in temperature. This high specific heat capacity (about 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, versus 385 for copper) is why water cools down and heats up more slowly than other materials and why oceans moderate climate.

questions.q: The conversion between the temperature scales is: degrees Kelvin = degrees Celsius + 273. What is the Kelvin temperature at which ice melts?
options: 0 K
questions.explanation: Ice melts at 0 °C, so the equivalent Kelvin temperature is 0 + 273 = 273 K. The increments on the Kelvin scale are the same size as those on the Celsius scale; only the zero point differs, with absolute zero (0 K) at about −273 °C.

questions.q: From memory: what is meant by thermal equilibrium, and which way does energy flow before it is reached?
keyPoints: Energy is always transferred from a region of high temperature to a region of lower temperature.
This continues until both regions reach the same (uniform) temperature.
When the temperature is uniform, a state of thermal equilibrium exists; the particles then have the same average random translational kinetic energy and there is no net transfer of energy.
questions.explanation: If you stated that energy flows from hot to cold until the temperatures are equal, and that equilibrium means equal temperatures (equal average particle kinetic energy) with no net transfer, grade yourself Good or Easy. Note a hot nail can transfer energy to water even though the water holds more total internal energy.

questions.q: How much energy is needed to heat 8.0 kg of water from a room temperature of 15 °C to 85 °C? Take the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Straight application of \(Q = mc\Delta T\). The temperature change is the rise of 70 °C, which equals 70 K — use the change, not the absolute temperature of 85 °C. This is the textbook's own sample problem.

questions.q: In one sentence each, define temperature and define heat, making the difference between them clear.
keyPoints: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance — a property the object has at an instant.
Heat is energy transferred from a hotter object to a colder object because of the temperature difference between them — energy in transit.
An object does not contain heat; it contains internal energy. Heat is the name for that energy while it is flowing.
questions.explanation: The classic error is using 'heat' and 'temperature' as synonyms. If you captured that temperature is average particle kinetic energy (a property) while heat is transferred energy due to a temperature difference, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: How much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 2.0 kg of water by 30 K? Take the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Identify the mass, specific heat and temperature change, then multiply the three together. \(\Delta T\) is the change of 30 K, not an absolute temperature — a common slip.

questions.q: Why does physics prefer the Kelvin scale over the Celsius scale when relating temperature to the kinetic energy of particles?
options: The Kelvin scale has larger degree increments, giving more precise readings
Kelvin temperature is directly proportional to the average kinetic energy of the particles, because its zero (absolute zero) is where particle motion is at its minimum
The Celsius scale cannot measure temperatures below the freezing point of water
Kelvin is the only scale in which water boils at exactly 100 degrees
questions.explanation: Absolute zero (0 K) is the temperature at which particle kinetic energy is at its minimum, so Kelvin temperature is directly proportional to average particle kinetic energy — double the kelvin temperature and you double the average kinetic energy. Celsius has its zero at the arbitrary freezing point of water, so it lacks this proportionality.

questions.q: Distinguish between heat and temperature, referring to the particles of a substance. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance; the higher the temperature, the faster the particles move on average. Heat is energy that is transferred from a hotter object to a colder object because of the temperature difference between them — that is, energy in transit. The key difference is that temperature is a property the object has at an instant (its average particle kinetic energy), whereas heat is energy flowing because of a temperature difference, not something the object contains.

criteria.descriptor: Defines temperature as the average kinetic energy of the particles.
Defines heat as energy transferred from hot to cold due to a temperature difference (energy in transit).
States the distinction clearly: temperature is a property; heat is transferred energy.

questions.explanation: The trap is treating the two words as synonyms. Marks reward the distinction between a property (temperature) and a transfer (heat).
